subject: Toward a more efficient analysis of QTL x covariate interactions

messages.author: 4719990e9dfe6605
messages.subject: Toward a more efficient analysis of QTL x covariate interactions
parts:
Dear Karl,

I am currently trying to conduct an eQTL analysis in Arabidopsis and
want to evaluate cytoplasm x eQTL interactions. Following the
examples in section 7.2 of the rQTL book on QTL x covariate
interactions I wrote the following loop:

k<-1

while(k<=25000){
out.a=scanone(dataIM, pheno.col=k, addcov=x, model=c("normal"),
method=c("hk"))
out.u=scanone(dataIM, pheno.col=k, addcov=x, intcovar=cyto,
model=c("normal"), method=c("hk"))
set.seed(54955149)
operm.a <- scanone(dataIM, pheno.col=k, addcov=x, model=c("normal"),
method=c("hk"), n.perm=1000, n.cluster=32)
set.seed(54955149)
operm.u <- scanone(dataIM, pheno.col=k, addcov=x, intcovar=cyto,
model=c("normal"), method=c("hk"), n.perm=1000, n.cluster=32)
out.u <- c(out.u, out.u-out.a, labels=c("f","i"))
operm.u <- cbind(operm.u, operm.u - operm.a, labels=c("f","i"))
a<-summary(out.u, perms=operm.u, pvalues=TRUE)
all<-cbind(all, a)
write.table(all, file = "eQTL_Cyto_normal_perm_25000_dry.txt",
quote=FALSE, row.name=FALSE)
k<-k+1}

Unfortunately, even with the 32 processors this analysis runs very
slowly. I was only able to complete about 350 phenotypes in 24
hours. I usually can complete about 5000 phenotypes in 24 hours with
one processor using the pheno.col=1:5000 option. Since my analysis
involves so many phenotypes (~75000), I am trying to figure out a way
that I can make the analysis more efficient, without creating many
scripts. Do you have any suggestions? In the end, I need to estimate
p-values in order to implement a False Discovery Rate.

Thank you very much,

David

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Toward a more efficient analysis of QTL x covariate interactions
parts:
I expect it's the permutations that are taking all the time?
I would first do the actual analysis and study it.

You have to expect the permutation tests to take a long time.
You'll need more processors.

karl

messages.subject: Re: Toward a more efficient analysis of QTL x covariate interactions
parts:
Thanks Karl!

I have been spending some more time on the problem and it appears that
I can accomplish the analysis using the pheno.col=1:25662 statement
(see code below). This is incredibly faster than running the
permutations one at a time in a loop. My concern is whether all the
phenotypes will start with the same seed. I know that starting with
the same seed is very important for comparing the two models and so I
wanted to check with you that what I am doing is correct. From quick
glances at the output for a few phenotypes, it appears that the
permutations all do start with the same seed. Here is the code:

out.a=scanone(dataIM, pheno.col=1:25662, addcov=x, model=c("normal"),
method=c("hk"))
out.u=scanone(dataIM, pheno.col=1:25662, addcov=x, intcovar=cyto,

operm.a <- scanone(dataIM, pheno.col=1:25662, addcov=x,
model=c("normal"), method=c("hk"), n.perm=1000, n.cluster=6)
set.seed(54955149)
operm.u <- scanone(dataIM, pheno.col=1:25662, addcov=x, intcovar=cyto,
model=c("normal"), method=c("hk"), n.perm=1000, n.cluster=6)

out.u <- c(out.u, out.u-out.a, labels=c("f","i"))
operm.u <- cbind(operm.u, operm.u - operm.a, labels=c("f","i"))

tabbycol_25662<-summary(out.u, perms=operm.u, format="tabByCol",
pvalues=TRUE, ci.function="lodint")

write.table(tabbycol_25662, file = "Tab_by_dry_SNP_cyto_25662.txt",
quote=FALSE, row.name=FALSE)

Thanks again,

David

messages.author: 96353e7106735838
messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Re: Toward a more efficient analysis of QTL x covariate interactions
parts:
The phenotypes will be permuted in parallel. There should be no problem doing it this way; in fact it is preferred (to maintain the correlations among phenotypes) should you want to make some correction for the search across phenotypes as well as the search across the genome.

karl

messages.subject: Re: Toward a more efficient analysis of QTL x covariate interactions
parts:
Dear Karl,

Sorry to be a bother again. I have now completed running the
interactive model for all of my transcription phenotypes. I could run
about 2500 in a batch given the memory constraints in R, but this was
still way faster than running the phenotypes one at a time in a loop.

I then went back to spot check to make sure that the results I
obtained through the batch runs matched with running the traits
individually. I set the same seed for the individual phenotype runs
as for the batch runs. However, for some reason I got different p-
values for the same QTLs in the batch and individual phenotype runs.
Is it possible that the permutations are different in the batch runs
and the individual phenotype runs, even if the seed is the same?

Thanks again,

David

parts:
Yes, they would be different. In the runs of individual phenotypes, the permutations for each phenotype would be distinct whereas in the batch runs they would be the same for all phenotypes.

karl

On Sep 5, 2012, at 5:01 PM, David Lowry wrote:

> Dear Karl,
>
> Sorry to be a bother again. I have now completed running the
> interactive model for all of my transcription phenotypes. I could run
> about 2500 in a batch given the memory constraints in R, but this was
> still way faster than running the phenotypes one at a time in a loop.
>
> I then went back to spot check to make sure that the results I
> obtained through the batch runs matched with running the traits
> individually. I set the same seed for the individual phenotype runs
> as for the batch runs. However, for some reason I got different p-
> values for the same QTLs in the batch and individual phenotype runs.
> Is it possible that the permutations are different in the batch runs
> and the individual phenotype runs, even if the seed is the same?
>
> Thanks again,
>
> David
>
> On Aug 28, 2:07 pm, David Lowry <davidbryantlo...@gmail.com> wrote:
>> Excellent!
>>
>> Thanks again Karl.
>>
>> David
>>
>> On Aug 27, 6:32 pm, Karl Broman <kbro...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>
>>
>>
>>
>>
>>
>>
>>> The phenotypes will be permuted in parallel. There should be no problem doing it this way; in fact it is preferred (to maintain the correlations among phenotypes) should you want to make some correction for the search across phenotypes as well as the search across the genome.
>>
>>> karl
>>
>>> On Aug 27, 2012, at 1:36 PM, David Lowry <davidbryantlo...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>
>>>> Thanks Karl!
>>
>>>> I have been spending some more time on the problem and it appears that
>>>> I can accomplish the analysis using the pheno.col=1:25662 statement
>>>> (see code below). This is incredibly faster than running the
>>>> permutations one at a time in a loop. My concern is whether all the
>>>> phenotypes will start with the same seed. I know that starting with
>>>> the same seed is very important for comparing the two models and so I
>>>> wanted to check with you that what I am doing is correct. From quick
>>>> glances at the output for a few phenotypes, it appears that the
>>>> permutations all do start with the same seed. Here is the code:
>>
>>>> out.a=scanone(dataIM, pheno.col=1:25662, addcov=x, model=c("normal"),
>>>> method=c("hk"))
>>>> out.u=scanone(dataIM, pheno.col=1:25662, addcov=x, intcovar=cyto,
>>>> model=c("normal"), method=c("hk"))
>>>> set.seed(54955149)
>>>> operm.a <- scanone(dataIM, pheno.col=1:25662, addcov=x,
>>>> model=c("normal"), method=c("hk"), n.perm=1000, n.cluster=6)
>>>> set.seed(54955149)
>>>> operm.u <- scanone(dataIM, pheno.col=1:25662, addcov=x, intcovar=cyto,
>>>> model=c("normal"), method=c("hk"), n.perm=1000, n.cluster=6)
>>>> out.u <- c(out.u, out.u-out.a, labels=c("f","i"))
>>>> operm.u <- cbind(operm.u, operm.u - operm.a, labels=c("f","i"))
>>>> tabbycol_25662<-summary(out.u, perms=operm.u, format="tabByCol",
>>>> pvalues=TRUE, ci.function="lodint")
>>
>>>> write.table(tabbycol_25662, file = "Tab_by_dry_SNP_cyto_25662.txt",
>>>> quote=FALSE, row.name=FALSE)
>>
>>>> Thanks again,
>>
>>>> David
>>
>>>> On Aug 27, 8:26 am, Karl Broman <kbro...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>>>> I expect it's the permutations that are taking all the time?
>>>>> I would first do the actual analysis and study it.
>>
>>>>> You have to expect the permutation tests to take a long time.
>>>>> You'll need more processors.
>>
>>>>> karl
>>
>>>>> On Aug 24, 2012, at 7:02 AM, David Lowry wrote:
>>
>>>>>> Dear Karl,
>>
>>>>>> I am currently trying to conduct an eQTL analysis in Arabidopsis and
>>>>>> want to evaluate cytoplasm x eQTL interactions. Following the
>>>>>> examples in section 7.2 of the rQTL book on QTL x covariate
>>>>>> interactions I wrote the following loop:
>>
>>>>>> k<-1
>>
>>>>>> while(k<=25000){
>>>>>> out.a=scanone(dataIM, pheno.col=k, addcov=x, model=c("normal"),
>>>>>> method=c("hk"))
>>>>>> out.u=scanone(dataIM, pheno.col=k, addcov=x, intcovar=cyto,
>>>>>> model=c("normal"), method=c("hk"))
>>>>>> set.seed(54955149)
>>>>>> operm.a <- scanone(dataIM, pheno.col=k, addcov=x, model=c("normal"),
>>>>>> method=c("hk"), n.perm=1000, n.cluster=32)
>>>>>> set.seed(54955149)
>>>>>> operm.u <- scanone(dataIM, pheno.col=k, addcov=x, intcovar=cyto,
>>>>>> model=c("normal"), method=c("hk"), n.perm=1000, n.cluster=32)
>>>>>> out.u <- c(out.u, out.u-out.a, labels=c("f","i"))
>>>>>> operm.u <- cbind(operm.u, operm.u - operm.a, labels=c("f","i"))
>>>>>> a<-summary(out.u, perms=operm.u, pvalues=TRUE)
>>>>>> all<-cbind(all, a)
>>>>>> write.table(all, file = "eQTL_Cyto_normal_perm_25000_dry.txt",
>>>>>> quote=FALSE, row.name=FALSE)
>>>>>> k<-k+1}

>>>>>> Unfortunately, even with the 32 processors this analysis runs very

>>>>>> that I can make the analysis more efficient, without creating many
>>>>>> scripts. Do you have any suggestions? In the end, I need to estimate

>>
>>>>>> Thank you very much,
>>
>>>>>> David
